name: Marco Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do live-line work on the suburban network, which means working on lines while the power's still on, from a bucket truck with insulated tools. We do it so a whole street of houses doesn't lose power while we change a fuse or a cutout. A normal day is two or three jobs around the ring road suburbs, a sandwich in the truck, and back at the depot by four. I like that it's exact, every move has a reason. What wears me out is traffic, honestly, more than the work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's in the bucket with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Usually Benny, he's been my partner for four years. We barely talk up there, we don't need to, I hold, he cuts, that kind of thing. On weekends I go fishing at the reservoir or work on an old motorbike I've been rebuilding for two years, and I've paid most of my flat off, so life's pretty settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd expect, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, most new stuff gets oversold. At the depot I'd say something like, told you, the bucket truck isn't going anywhere. I don't post online, so nothing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life stays how I like it. Same jobs, same partner, same reservoir on Sundays. I've had the same pair of rubber gloves tested every month for years, and nobody's going to replace that with a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working, keep paying off the flat, I'd like it clear in about three years. Maybe finally finish the motorbike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a Sunday at the reservoir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My phone has some assistant thing on it and I turned it off. I don't need a machine guessing what I want to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe the company finds some other new thing to spend money on that doesn't work. But that happens every year anyway.

S0.say: He'd say he's not surprised because most new things are oversold, and tell the depot the bucket truck isn't going anywhere. He doesn't post online.
S0.think: His life stays exactly as he likes it, with the same jobs, partner and Sunday fishing. Nothing about his monthly-tested gloves gets replaced by a chatbot.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and keeps paying off his flat, aiming to clear it in about three years. Plans to finally finish rebuilding his motorbike.
S0.feel: Calm, like a Sunday at the reservoir.
S0.quote: I've had the same pair of rubber gloves tested every month for years, and nobody's going to replace that with a chatbot.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is settled and quietly sure of himself. He has switched off the AI assistant on his phone and sees no reason to use any of it. His satisfaction comes from routine and exactness, and he barely needs to talk to his bucket partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That's more realistic. I don't love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we'll see, they always bring in new stuff and half of it doesn't stick. To friends I'd say my job's hands-on so I'm probably okay. I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the company would start pushing tablets and tracking and new procedures, and I'd hate that. I'd still have a job, but it would feel less like mine. I don't mind change at the edges, I mind someone rewriting the steps I know by heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and see what actually changes before I do anything. If they made the new training compulsory, I'd do it, but I wouldn't volunteer. I'd keep paying off the flat so if things go sideways I've got no rent. That's my safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like someone moving the furniture around in your house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they changed the steps, what would that look like on a normal job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Say they bring in a system that tells you the order to do things on a live line. I've got my own order, I check, double-check, then move. If a screen tells me to skip a step to save time, I'd ignore it, and that's when you get in trouble with management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planners and the stores guys, probably. Benny would be fine, he's good with phones. Me, I'd be fine too, just grumpy.

S1.say: He'd tell the depot they'll see, because half of new things don't stick, and tell friends his hands-on job is probably okay. He wouldn't make a big deal of it.
S1.think: The company would push tablets, tracking and new procedures, making the job feel less like his. He minds someone rewriting steps he knows by heart.
S1.do: Keeps working as he is and waits to see what changes, doing compulsory training only if required. Keeps paying down his flat so he'd have no rent if things go wrong.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like someone moving the furniture in his house.
S1.quote: I don't mind change at the edges, I mind someone rewriting the steps I know by heart.
S1.fieldNote: Marco's worry is about control of his own routine, not losing his job. He is clear he would not volunteer for training. His paid-down flat is his real safety net and he mentions it as his main plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? No. That's crazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it, probably, at least at first. At the depot I'd say show me a robot that can do live-line work in the rain. I'd keep it quiet with friends, I'm not the type to make speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if it really happened, I'd be in trouble. I don't know anything else, I've done lines since I was nineteen. I'd have a flat with no mortgage and nothing to do between waking up and the reservoir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on the motorbike and anything extra, and throw everything at the flat so it's fully paid. That's step one. Then I'd wait and see if they really lay us off, because the company would need people at first to watch the robots. I wouldn't know what else to do, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Like the bucket jerks and you don't know why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. Is that because you think it won't happen, or because you don't know what else to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I keep thinking it won't, but if it does, I wouldn't know where to start. I'm not going to become a computer guy at twenty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years take away from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Any chance to get used to it. Two years is nothing. I'd still be finishing the flat payments when the robots turned up at the depot.

S2.say: He'd say he doesn't believe it at first and challenge anyone to show him a robot doing live-line work in the rain. He'd keep quiet with friends.
S2.think: If it happened he'd be in real trouble, since lines are all he's done since nineteen. He pictures a paid-off flat and nothing to fill his days.
S2.do: Stops spending on the motorbike and extras and puts everything into paying off the flat. Then waits to see whether layoffs actually come, unsure what else he would do.
S2.feel: Bad, like a bucket jerking with no explanation.
S2.quote: I'd have a flat with no mortgage and nothing to do between waking up and the reservoir.
S2.fieldNote: Marco's first reaction is disbelief, and his plan beyond paying off the flat is to wait. He admits he wouldn't know where to start and rules out retraining. The strong savings protect his home, but not his sense of purpose, which is what really shakes him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still not long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when I see it. Maybe at the depot I'd start asking the managers what the plan is. I still wouldn't say much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means the flat's paid off for sure, that's something. But I'd still have nothing to do after. Five years sounds long until you realise that's just two more motorbike rebuilds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the flat early and keep saving the extra. I'd keep working, of course. Maybe in the last year or two I'd look at what jobs are left, but I'd wait until I could see it was really coming. I might ask the union what they're doing, but I wouldn't lead anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still pretty worried. Less of a shock, but the same feeling underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your days, if the work stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Fishing, the motorbike, maybe help my dad with his garden. But that's not a life at twenty-eight or thirty-two, that's retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat, basically. With two years it's close, with five it's done. It doesn't buy me a new job, because I'd still be waiting.

S3.say: He'd say he'll believe it when he sees it, though he might start asking managers what the plan is. He still wouldn't say much online.
S3.think: Five years guarantees the flat is paid off, but he'd still have nothing to do afterwards. It feels like just two more motorbike rebuilds.
S3.do: Pays off his flat early and saves the extra while working as usual. Waits until the change is clearly coming before looking at other jobs, and might ask the union what it's doing without leading anything.
S3.feel: Still worried, less shocked, with the same feeling underneath.
S3.quote: Five years sounds long until you realise that's just two more motorbike rebuilds.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time mainly buys Marco a paid-off home, not a new path. He is honest that he would still wait rather than act. His fear is about empty days and losing his place in the world, not about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a lot can change in ten years, so let's not get carried away. At the depot I'd probably joke I'll retire before the robots learn to climb. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'd get some good years of the job I like. I'd be thirty-seven, and that's still young enough to do something else, but I don't know what. Ten years is enough time to finish everything I've started and still not have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and finish the flat, then save hard for a few years. Maybe at some point I'd think about some other hands-on work, like fixing machines, if anything's still left for people. I'd watch what other guys do first. I'm not going to rush off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's farther off. Easier to push to the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd watch what others do first. Is that a plan, or a way to put it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a way to put it off, if I'm honest. I know myself, I'm slow to move. But I've also seen people jump at every new thing and get burned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra five years change for you, compared with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly it gives me more money in the bank and more years of a job I like. It doesn't change who I am. I'd still be the guy waiting.

S4.say: He'd say a lot can change in ten years and joke at the depot that he'll retire before the robots learn to climb. He'd say nothing online.
S4.think: He'd get good years of a job he likes, and at 37 he'd still be young enough to change, but he has no idea what to. Ten years might pass without a plan.
S4.do: Keeps working, finishes paying off the flat and saves hard for a few years. Considers other hands-on work like fixing machines at some point, but only after watching what others do first.
S4.feel: Worried but further off, easier to push to the back of his mind.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time to finish everything I've started and still not have a plan.
S4.fieldNote: When I asked whether watching others was a plan or a delay, Marco admitted it was a delay. He is self-aware about being slow to move and points to people who got burned by rushing. More time means more money and more years of work he likes, but no change in how he'd respond.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. In the others at least I'd finish the flat and have more time to get used to it. I can handle not having a job for a while, what I can't handle is not knowing what I'm for. What would help is the company keeping people on to work alongside the robots, even fewer of us, so the ones who know the lines aren't just thrown away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people like me would do with the time. Everyone talks about money, but I've got money. It's the days I'd worry about.

headlineQuote: I can handle not having a job for a while, what I can't handle is not knowing what I'm for.
portrait: Marco Tanaka is a 27-year-old live-line worker on a suburban network who works from a bucket truck with his partner Benny and spends weekends fishing or rebuilding an old motorbike. He has nearly paid off his flat, never uses AI tools and has switched off the assistant on his phone. He is calm in the plateau, uneasy that steady disruption would rewrite the steps he knows by heart, and alarmed by AGI in two or five years. Even with ten years he admits he would mostly wait and watch others, because his deepest fear is not money but empty days without purpose.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he would have no time to finish his flat or get used to it, and he fears not knowing what he's for.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping some experienced lineworkers on to work alongside the robots, so the people who know the lines aren't thrown away.
